title: The NRI's Guide to Japan — Bullet Trains, Cherry Blossoms, and the Safest Country You Will Ever Visit
excerpt: Trains arrive to the second. Convenience stores stock restaurant-quality food. Toilets have more buttons than your car.
body:
## Why Japan?

Japan is the trip that changes how you think about civilisation. For NRIs accustomed to both American efficiency and Indian chaos, Japan operates on a plane that makes both look amateurish. Trains arrive to the second. Convenience stores stock restaurant-quality food. Toilets have more buttons than your car. And beneath this technological precision lies a culture of such depth — tea ceremonies, Zen gardens, samurai castles, anime districts — that two weeks feels like barely scratching the surface. Japan has gone from "someday" to "this year" for Indian Americans, driven by direct flights, a weak yen, and Instagram-fuelled cherry blossom mania.

## Top Experiences

**1. Tokyo: Shibuya, Shinjuku & Senso-ji** — Watch the world's busiest intersection at Shibuya Crossing from the Starbucks above. Explore Shinjuku's neon-lit alleys and Golden Gai's tiny six-seat bars. Senso-ji temple in Asakusa is Tokyo's oldest and most atmospheric.

**2. Kyoto: Fushimi Inari & Arashiyama** — Ten thousand vermillion torii gates winding up Mount Inari is Japan's most photographed sight. Arashiyama's bamboo grove and the golden Kinkaku-ji temple are equally mandatory. Rent a kimono for the day — it is not cultural appropriation in Japan; it is celebrated.

**3. Osaka: Street Food Capital** — Dōtonbori is Japan's greatest food street. Takoyaki (octopus balls), okonomiyaki (savoury pancakes), and gyoza are all must-eats. Osaka Castle is impressive but the city is really about eating your way through it.

**4. Hiroshima Peace Memorial & Miyajima Island** — The Peace Memorial Museum is sobering and essential. Combine with a ferry to Miyajima Island to see the floating torii gate of Itsukushima Shrine — one of Japan's most iconic images.

**5. Mount Fuji & Hakone** — On a clear day, Mount Fuji from Hakone's Lake Ashi is the quintessential Japan photo. Take the Romancecar train from Shinjuku, cruise the lake, ride the ropeway over volcanic steam vents, and soak in an onsen (hot spring bath) overnight.

## Getting There

Direct flights from the US to Tokyo Narita/Haneda on ANA, JAL, United, Delta, and American. Flight time is 12–14 hours from the West Coast, 14–16 from the East Coast. The Japan Rail Pass (7/14/21 days) is essential — it covers bullet trains (Shinkansen), local trains, and some ferries. Buy before arriving. The Tokyo–Kyoto bullet train takes 2 hours 15 minutes and runs every 10 minutes. Japan's rail system is the best in the world — you will not need a car.

## Where to Stay

Tokyo: Shinjuku for transit hub convenience, Shibuya for energy, Asakusa for traditional atmosphere. Park Hyatt Tokyo (from Lost in Translation) for luxury, Dormy Inn chain for onsen-equipped business hotels. Kyoto: Stay near Gion (geisha district) or Higashiyama. A ryokan (traditional inn) with tatami rooms, futon beds, and kaiseki dinner is a must-do at least one night — budget ¥15,000–40,000/person. Osaka: Namba or Shinsaibashi. Japan has excellent capsule hotels ($30–50) and hostels for budget travellers.

## Food & the Desi Connection

Japanese food is technically the furthest from Indian cuisine you can get — no spices, no oil, no chillies — and yet Indian Americans consistently fall in love with it. Sushi, ramen, tempura, and curry rice are the big four. Yes, Japan has its own curry — sweeter and milder than Indian curry, served everywhere from convenience stores to speciality shops (CoCo Ichibanya chain is everywhere). Vegetarians face the biggest challenge — dashi (fish stock) is in nearly everything. Learn the phrase "niku nashi, sakana nashi" (no meat, no fish) and seek out shojin ryori (Buddhist temple cuisine) for authentic vegan meals. Convenience store (konbini) food — onigiri, sandwiches, bento boxes — is shockingly good and cheap (¥100–500).

## NRI Tips

Indian passport holders need a visa — apply at the Japanese consulate, processed in 5–7 business days. US citizens get 90 days visa-free. Currency is Japanese Yen (¥) — $1 ≈ ¥155. Japan is still heavily cash-based outside major cities — carry ¥10,000–20,000 daily. 7-Eleven ATMs accept international cards. Japan is the safest country most people will ever visit — violent crime is essentially zero, lost wallets are returned with cash intact. Tipping is not done and can cause confusion. Shoes off indoors — always. Tattoos: many traditional onsen (hot springs) still ban tattooed guests — ask before booking. Cherry blossom season (late March to mid-April) is peak season — book 3–4 months ahead. Autumn foliage (November) is equally spectacular and less crowded.
